artists.biography:
Jean Michel André Jarre (born 24 August 1948 in Lyon) is a French composer, performer and music producer. He is a pioneer in the electronic, ambient and New Age genres, and known as an organiser of outdoor spectacles of his music featuring lights, laser displays, and fireworks.

Jarre was raised in Lyon by his mother and grandparents, and trained on the piano. From an early age he was introduced to a variety of art forms, including those of street performers, jazz musicians, and the artist Pierre Soulages. He played guitar in a band, but his musical style was perhaps most heavily influenced by Pierre Schaeffer, a pioneer of musique concrète at the Groupe de Recherches Musicales.

His first mainstream success was the 1976 album Oxygène. Recorded in a makeshift studio at his home, the album sold an estimated 12 million copies. Oxygène was followed in 1978 by Équinoxe, and in 1979 Jarre performed to a record-breaking audience of more than a million people at the Place de la Concorde, a record he has since broken three times. More albums were to follow, but his 1979 concert served as a blueprint for his future performances around the world. Several of his albums have been released to coincide with large-scale outdoor events, and he is now perhaps as well known as a performer as a musician.

As of 2004 Jarre had sold an estimated 80 million albums. He was the first Western musician to be allowed to perform in the People's Republic of China, and holds the world record for the largest-ever audience at an outdoor event.

perplexity.description:
Magnetic Fields is the sixth studio album by Jean-Michel Jarre, released in May 1981 under the title Les Chants Magnétiques in France. The album represents a significant evolution in Jarre's electronic music practice, showcasing a colder, more digital aesthetic than his previous works while incorporating sampling as a musical element—making it one of the first albums to employ sampling in this way. Structured as five interconnected parts that flow seamlessly together, the album explores themes of magnetism, technology, and their impact on human experience in an increasingly digital world.

Musically, Magnetic Fields is characterized by extensive use of analog synthesizers, sequencers, and complex rhythmic patterns that create a hypnotic, futuristic soundscape. The album balances an extended electronic excursion in the opening movement with shorter, more accessible pieces in its second half. Standout tracks include the radio-friendly "Magnetic Fields Part 2" and "Magnetic Fields Part 4," while "Magnetic Fields Part 3" draws comparisons to German electronic pioneers like Kraftwerk and Cluster through its luminous, playful textures featuring toy and train sounds. The album concludes with "The Last Rumba," a contrasting diversion that provides a memorable closing statement.

The album achieved notable commercial success, reaching number 6 on the UK charts and number 98 on the US charts. Magnetic Fields is regarded as among Jarre's most artistically interesting works, demonstrating his continued innovation within electronic music while maintaining the accessibility that had made his earlier albums like Oxygène (1976) and Equinoxe (1978) international successes.
